passage: I'm Nikita, and at fifteen I was furious that my mother, Tanuja, wanted me home by eight every evening. It felt like being handed back to primary school. I didn't shout. I just answered in single words, took my dinner to my room and shut the door a little too firmly. For two days I stewed. Then I noticed I was only making my own evenings worse. On the third night I said, "Mummy, being home by eight means I miss the last hour of dance practice every day. Can we try later for two weeks, and I'll message you when I leave? If it goes badly, we go back." She was quiet, then said, "Two weeks. Let's see." I'd expected an argument and got a trial instead.

qa.q: What time did Tanuja want Nikita home every evening?
qa.a: She wanted her home by eight every evening.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling during the two days she answered in single words?
qa.a: She was angry and resentful at being treated like a small child, and she kept it inside instead of saying it.

qa.q: What made Nikita's approach on the third night work better than sulking?
qa.a: She calmly named what the rule cost her, dance practice, and offered a trial with messages, so her mother had something concrete to agree to. 🙂

qa.q: How might Tanuja have seen Nikita's shut door before the talk?
qa.a: Probably as a sign her daughter was upset without knowing why, which may have made her worry more, so a clear request gave her something she could respond to.

grounding: Shows a teen resenting a curfew, first sulking silently, then calmly stating the cost and proposing a trial of trust.

passage: I'm Karthik, Asif's classmate, and I was at his flat on Saturday doing our project when his father knocked. "Text me when you reach the library. And wear the helmet, please." Asif answered without looking up. "Papa, nobody does that anymore." After the door closed he muttered, "Stuck in the nineties. He thinks the road is a war zone." He picked up his phone and read a message out loud in a silly voice: "Take the jacket, it's cold." Then he stopped, and I saw him look at the closed door. "His friend had an accident once," he said quietly. "That's why." He put on the jacket anyway. I honestly can't tell whether he was more annoyed or worried.

qa.q: What did Asif's father ask him to do when he reached the library?
qa.a: He asked him to text when he reached the library.

qa.q: What might Asif have been feeling when he stopped mocking the message and looked at the closed door?
qa.a: Possibly a flicker of understanding, since he mentioned his father's friend's accident, though Karthik admits he can't tell if Asif was more annoyed or worried.

qa.q: What could Asif try next time his father sets a rule like this?
qa.a: He could keep his father's worry in mind while suggesting an easier way to check in, so they can talk about the fear and not just the method.

qa.q: How might Asif's father feel when his son sneers at the rule?
qa.a: Possibly hurt or brushed aside, even though the rule comes from fear for his son's safety.

grounding: Shows a teen sneering at his father's rules as outdated, an observer seeing him briefly separate the fear behind the rule from the method.

passage:
Trisha: Reached Meera's 🙂
Deepika: Good. Text when you leave. Don't take an auto after dark.
Trisha: Mummy, can I ask something? What exactly are you scared of?
Deepika: Accidents. Some stranger. People talking if you're out late.
Trisha: Okay. That's actually clear. I thought you just didn't trust me.
Deepika: It's never that. I picture the worst and my chest goes tight.
Trisha: What if I share my live location till I'm home, and call from the gate?
Deepika: That would help a lot.
Trisha: Deal. Love you ❤️
Deepika: Love you too. Eat something there.

qa.q: What did Deepika say she was afraid of?
qa.a: She said she feared accidents, some stranger, and people talking if Trisha was out late.

qa.q: What did Trisha think her mother's rules meant before she asked what exactly she feared?
qa.a: She thought her mother just didn't trust her, and hearing the actual fears showed her it was worry and love.

qa.q: How did Trisha's suggestion address her mother's fear?
qa.a: Sharing her live location and calling from the gate answers the specific worry about the trip home, so the rule can loosen without ignoring the fear. 🙂

qa.q: What is it like for Deepika when her daughter goes out?
qa.a: She pictures the worst and her chest goes tight, so the rules are how her anxiety and love show up.

grounding: Shows a teen recognising that rules come from love plus anxiety and asking what her mother fears so it can be addressed.

passage: In the sports club office, Noor stood in front of Coach Thomas with the permission form still blank. "I can't come to the weekend camp. My parents said no." Thomas raised an eyebrow. "You look unhappy about it." "I am. I think they're being overcautious. I told them so." She looked at her shoes. "But last year they said no to the trip with the older group, and it turned out the bus company had lost its licence. They've been right when it mattered, so I'm going to trust them." "And will you leave it there?" "No. I'm going to ask if I can do the day camp in spring and see if they'll say yes." Thomas nodded slowly. "That sounds fair."

qa.q: What did Noor say her parents had said no to last year?
qa.a: They said no to the trip with the older group.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling about her parents' refusal, and why did she still follow it?
qa.a: She was unhappy and thought they were overcautious, but she followed it because they had proved right when it mattered.

qa.q: What did Noor plan to do after accepting the no?
qa.a: She planned to ask her parents if she could do the day camp in spring, so she speaks up for her wishes without breaking the rule. 🙂

qa.q: How might Coach Thomas see Noor's decision?
qa.a: He likely sees a mature teenager who complies but doesn't just swallow her disappointment, which is why he called her plan fair.

grounding: Shows a teen following a parental rule she dislikes because of earned trust, saying so openly and negotiating for later.

passage: Chandrika had a system. A few sniffles at the dinner table got her the sleepover. "You're the best Mummy in the world" got her the extra pocket money. It worked more often than not, and afterwards she always felt faintly slippery, like she had handed over a coin she'd made from cardboard. When the school trip to Jaipur came up, she opened her mouth to start the sniffling and stopped. Her brother Amandeep, at the other end of the sofa, raised an eyebrow. Instead, she laid the teacher's letter on the table. "It's with two teachers, the hotel is near the school's usual one, and I'll call every night. Can I go?" Her father read it twice. "Ask me tomorrow." She was surprised how steady her hands were.

qa.q: Where was the school trip going?
qa.a: The school trip was going to Jaipur.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel after her sniffling and flattery had worked?
qa.a: She felt faintly slippery, as if she had paid with a coin made of cardboard.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do differently for the Jaipur trip, and why might it earn more freedom?
qa.a: She made an honest case with the teacher's letter and a plan to call every night, which builds trust her parents can rely on.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Chandrika's usual routine?
qa.a: He seems to know it well, since he raised an eyebrow when she opened her mouth, so he may see it as a habit that could wear thin.

grounding: Shows a teen who fakes tears and flattery to get permission, feels slippery, and makes an honest case instead.

passage: I'm Jaya, and last year my father, Gautam, changed the rules almost overnight. I'd started at a new school, gone quiet at home and stopped saying where I was going. He began texting every hour, then decided I couldn't go out after school at all. At first I only felt watched. Later I realised he looked shut out, standing by the door when I came in. So I tried something. Before he could ask, I'd say, "Going to the library with Anu, back by six." Then a photo of the shelf. It felt silly at first. After some weeks he stopped texting. One evening he said, "You don't have to tell me everything, but thank you." I felt lighter, and so, I think, did he.

qa.q: What did Gautam do when Jaya stopped saying where she was going?
qa.a: He began texting every hour and then decided she couldn't go out after school.

qa.q: How did Jaya's father seem to feel, judging by the way he stood at the door?
qa.a: He looked shut out and worried, waiting for her to tell him what was happening in her life.

qa.q: What did Jaya do that changed things, and why did it help?
qa.a: She told him her plans before he asked, which lowered his need to check and let her earn more freedom.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt when she told him about her plans?
qa.a: Probably relieved and reassured, because it answered his worry and made him feel included again.

grounding: Shows a teen whose parent clamps down out of worry and who shares plans freely to reduce the need to control.

passage:
Dear Mummy,

I'm writing this because I get tongue-tied when we talk. I know you check my phone each night, and that you started after the group chat mess. I understand you were scared. But it makes me feel watched, and I've started deleting messages just to feel private, which I don't like doing.

Can you tell me exactly what you're worried about? I'll show you my chats myself on Sunday evenings for now, and I promise I won't make secret accounts. Could we look at it again in a couple of months, and if I've been open, you check less?

Thanks for reading this. 🙂

Sarika

P.S. I'll be in the kitchen. Irawati Auntie next door says hi.

qa.q: On which evenings does Sarika offer to show her chats?
qa.a: She offers to show them on Sunday evenings.

qa.q: What is Sarika feeling about the nightly phone checks, and how does she show it?
qa.a: She feels watched and uneasy, and it shows in how she has started deleting messages just to feel private.

qa.q: What is Sarika doing that could help build trust with her mother?
qa.a: She asks for a clear reason, promises no secret accounts, shares her chats openly and suggests a review in a couple of months, so constant checking becomes less needed.

qa.q: How might Sarika's mother feel when she reads the letter?
qa.a: Probably relieved that her daughter is talking openly, and maybe a little sad to hear the checking hurt, while still worried about what caused it.

grounding: Shows a teen whose phone is monitored writing to ask for a clear reason and a path to more trust, sharing openly and promising no secret accounts.

passage:
"Sneha scored ninety-six in maths," said Aai, ladling dal. "Why can't you be like her?"
"Aai, please."
"I'm only saying."
Sarika put her spoon down. Later, on the terrace, she said to Masi, "When Aai says that, I feel like something's wrong with me. Like she only loves me at ninety-six."
"Does she?"
"I don't know. I know it feels like it."
"Then tell her that, the way you just told me."
"She'll say I'm being dramatic."
"Maybe. But you don't have to believe the comparison. What's your own goal?"
"Get science up first. Then maths."
"Good. Say that to her too."

qa.q: What did Sneha score in maths?
qa.a: She scored ninety-six in maths.

qa.q: What does Sarika's remark that she feels like Aai only loves her at ninety-six say about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels small and defective, as though her mother's love depends on marks, though she isn't sure if it's true.

qa.q: What could Sarika do next after talking to Masi?
qa.a: She could tell Aai how the comparison lands and share her own goals, science first, then maths, without treating the comparison as truth about her worth.

qa.q: How might Aai see her remark about Sneha?
qa.a: Probably as a push to do better, not realising it lands as a judgement on Sarika's worth.

grounding: Shows a teen feeling small when compared to a topper cousin, naming the hurt to a trusted adult and holding her own goals.

passage: I'm Usha, and for most of Class 10 I disliked my cousin Imran, which was unfair because he never did anything except lend me his notes. Every time we visited, Mama would say, "Imran has topped again," and something in me hardened. I stopped revising for the maths test. Not because I couldn't, but to make a point. The point lasted until I got the paper back. Nobody was hurt except me. That night I said, "Mama, when you compare me with Imran it feels like a race I never signed up for. Can you help me set my own target and check in on it?" She looked stunned, then said, "I didn't know it sounded like that." We picked a number for the next test that was mine.

qa.q: What did Usha stop doing before the maths test?
qa.a: She stopped revising.

qa.q: Why did Usha dislike Imran, even though he had done nothing wrong?
qa.a: She resented her mother's comparisons and let that resentment land on Imran, who was simply the person she was compared with.

qa.q: What did Usha do that worked better than sabotaging her own test?
qa.a: She calmly told her mother how comparison lands and asked for help setting her own target. 🙂

qa.q: How might Imran feel if he knew Usha had disliked him?
qa.a: Probably confused and hurt, since he only lent her his notes and had no part in the comparisons.

grounding: Shows a teen resenting a parent's comparisons, quietly disliking the cousin and sabotaging her own work, then telling the parent how it lands.

passage: Ishita, I saw your face at the Diwali dinner when Aunty announced your cousin's marks and then asked what you'd got. I'm Pranav, your Mama, and I remember that hot, sinking feeling. At your age I was the one compared aloud to my elder brother, in front of half our relatives. I went red and stared at my plate. What I understood later was that my mother's pride and worry were leaking out of her, and I happened to be standing there. It was never about my worth. So talk to your mother privately, not at the party. Tell her it hurts to be measured out loud. Then show her your effort your own way. I'll be nearby if you'd like company.

qa.q: Who announced the cousin's marks at the Diwali dinner?
qa.a: Aunty announced them.

qa.q: What did young Pranav feel when he was compared aloud to his brother?
qa.a: He felt hot and sunk, going red and staring at his plate, judged in front of relatives.

qa.q: What could Ishita do about being compared at family gatherings?
qa.a: She can ask her mother privately to stop measuring her out loud and show her effort in her own way.

qa.q: How might Ishita's mother feel about the comparison at the dinner?
qa.a: Her pride and anxiety were probably driving it, so she may not realise how much it stings, which is why a private talk could help. 🤍

grounding: Shows an elder telling a teen about being compared aloud, that it comes from adults' pride and anxiety, and advising a private request to stop.
